paras: The killing of Canny Clark was the shooting of a Black man by Sheriff H. C. Griffin and a posse at daybreak on Tuesday, July 31, 1900, near Dade City, Florida. According to the only report, Clark drew a revolver on the sheriff and the posse shot him dead, and an inquest returned a verdict of justifiable homicide.
The Savannah Morning News described Clark as "a negro desperado," but it named no crime he was accused of and did not say why the sheriff's posse was out.

The encounter took place on a road near the turpentine camp of Allison & Gasque, not far from Dade City. In the paper's words, the posse met Clark "by chance" on the road. By the officers' account as printed, Clark "immediately drew his revolver and attempted to shoot the sheriff," and the posse "riddled him with buckshot." No witness other than the posse is quoted, and the size of the posse is not given.
An inquest found the killing to be justifiable homicide. The coverage gives no details of the inquest and reports no arrests or further proceedings.

The killing appears in a single four-sentence item in the Savannah Morning News of August 3, 1900, on page 6, under the headline "Killed a Desperado." The item presented the posse's version without attribution, called Clark a "negro desperado," and closed with the inquest verdict. No other white paper and no Black paper in the coverage reported the killing, so the posse's account stands unchallenged and unconfirmed.

bases: A sheriff and his posse shot and killed Clark on a road when they met him, by their account after he drew a revolver (A1).

Clark was killed by a sheriff's posse of unstated size, and the only account is the officers' version that he drew a revolver first, endorsed by an inquest verdict of justifiable homicide (A1). Nothing in the single report shows whether the killing was lawful or extralegal.
One short item in the Savannah Morning News is the only report found in either press (A1).
